svg.text: Algorithmics (MTAT.03.238) · Institute of Computer Science · November 2026
A clash-free weekly timetable for a 100-class school in 1 second, polished in 10 seconds.
Schools in Kazakhstan still build timetables by hand: 20–100 classes in grades 5–11, up
to 170 teachers, two shifts, subgroup lessons with two teachers.
Clashes alone already make it graph colouring (lessons are vertices, a shared class or
teacher is an edge, slots are colours), so the problem is NP-hard.
no clash for a class or a teacher; every lesson placed
class stays inside its shift and has no gaps in its day
teacher is not booked when unavailable

text.tspan: Soft rules: weighted penalty to minimise

svg.text: same subject twice a day; hard subjects late, easy ones early
uneven daily difficulty by the official subject scores (ҚР ДСМ-76 [6])
teacher gaps (squared), switches between shifts, broken teacher wishes
Place the lesson with the fewest
free slots first, into its cheapest
Move a lesson, swap two lessons of
a class, or swap a Kempe chain.
Annealing starts from the DSATUR timetable and accepts a worse one with probability
exp(−Δ/T), T = 20 → 1, 1000 moves per lesson. A broken hard rule costs 1000, so the
search may pass through infeasible timetables and repair them.
a line = same class or same teacher; blue lessons swap slots together
Take two slots and one lesson in them, then everything linked to it by a shared class or
teacher. Swapping the whole chain never creates a clash. Chains are short: median 2

text.tspan: Kempe chains make dense schools feasible

svg.text: 64 schools with a feasible timetable proved by HiGHS; the busiest teacher is booked up to 97 % of the week. Final weights,
same set for all three. At equal running time Kempe chains also lower the soft cost by about 15 %, more than all parameter

text.tspan: Annealing beats tabu search at equal time

svg.text: Soft cost per 100 lessons, lower is better; 30 normal and 64 dense schools, same moves and same time. Tabu search
spends 100 evaluations per step, annealing one, so annealing takes 100× more steps.

text.tspan: Quality grows with time, size is not a problem

svg.text: 100-class school, one shift. Running time grows linearly with the number of lessons: 7 s for 60 classes, 10 s for 100.
Common cost that both programs can express (no difficulty rules), costs re-checked by our XHSTT evaluator; the better
result is shaded. KHE wins on one-shift schools, annealing wins on two-shift schools and is 3–13× faster.

text.tspan: What we do not know yet

svg.text: All schools are generated from real curricula and rules; no real school has been
The weights encode our priorities; only a deputy head can confirm them.
Distance to the optimum: best lower bound 42 vs our 75 on the smallest school.
HSEval sees up to a third of the soft cost: daily difficulty and half-day rules are not
exported, they are cross-checked by our exact model only.
We wrote a reader and a writer for XHSTT, the standard format of school timetabling, and ran our
timetables through HSEval. It accepted every file and re-scored every timetable to the same
numbers. Our reader also loads all 25 schools of the public XHSTT archive.
timetables: the validator's cost equals ours, to the point
schools, 100 classes included: zero hard violations in our annealing
hard rules, repeats, teacher gaps, shifts and wishes agree in our solver,
Build your own school and watch DSATUR, annealing and
Kempe chains work step by step. Same code as the solver.
